case_study_insert.main_stem: Aurora Hydrogen (AHY) is a public limited company in the hydrogen refuelling sector, operating a green-hydrogen truck refuelling station on the national industrial corridor. Founded in 2021 by Dr Elena Vasquez, it employs a workforce of 22 and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership among its engineers. AHY plans to invest $640,000 in a second high-pressure dispenser and a mobile refuelling trailer for HGV fleet trials, financed by a $340,000 share issue and $300,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $176,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.30 a unit and a selling price of $9.50, and currently produces 78,000 units a year. AHY faces one operational problem: a skills gap, as 16 of its 22 staff have not completed high-pressure hydrogen safety certification.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — October 2026 (n = 210 HGV fleet managers): 68% would trial hydrogen trucks within 24 months if corridor refuelling is reliable; 54% would pay up to $0.60 more per kg for guaranteed green hydrogen; 47% cite lack of refuelling infrastructure as the main barrier. Pilot operations ran 1,380 kg of hydrogen through the dispenser in Q3 2026 with zero customer complaints and an average refuelling time of 11 minutes. 16 of 22 staff have not completed high-pressure hydrogen safety certification; courses at the energy skills centre cost $950 per employee. A training needs analysis found that drivers and dispenser technicians need on-the-job training on hydrogen safety and off-the-job training on high-pressure refuelling certification before the corridor depot opens.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Aurora Hydrogen for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The government has increased the carbon levy on diesel by 8.2% from January 2027, raising running costs for conventional HGV fleets. (2) Electricity input costs for electrolysis have risen 13.7% year-on-year, raising green-hydrogen production costs. (3) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.5% to 6.25%, increasing borrowing costs for capital-intensive energy businesses.

questions.question_text: AHY plans to fund the second high-pressure dispenser with a $340,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for AHY of using the share issue to fund the expansion rather than additional bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $340,000 share issue raises permanent capital without interest or a fixed repayment schedule, which matters for a public limited company whose operating margin is only 14.0% in 2025 and whose cash must absorb the 13.7% rise in electrolysis electricity costs. Unlike a bank loan repriced after the base rate move to 6.25%, shares carry no compulsory cash drain each month, preserving the headroom AHY needs while the corridor's HGV trials scale through 1,380 kg of hydrogen a quarter.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads the risk of an unproven hydrogen corridor across outside investors rather than concentrating it with lenders who can force repayment or covenant breaches. Public money also adds credibility with fleet customers and the grid connection authority, signals market confidence in Dr Vasquez's 2021 vision, and aligns shareholders with the green-hydrogen growth story; the trade-off is dividend expectations and some dilution of existing stakes, which patient growth investors accept.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Aurora Hydrogen and its second dispenser decision.

questions.question_text: AHY is launching its second high-pressure dispenser and mobile refuelling trailer for HGV fleet trials. Consider a consumer-style social media campaign, an industry white paper mailed to HGV fleet managers, or open-day demonstrations for fleet operators at the corridor station. Which should AHY choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Consumer-style social media campaign: Short videos of trucks refuelling in 11 minutes would build broad awareness cheaply and humanise the green-hydrogen story for the public and local councillors. But HGV fleet managers, the people who actually sign fuel contracts, do not buy hydrogen because of their newsfeed; social platforms cannot demonstrate 350-bar dispensing safety or answer technical procurement questions, so reach would be high and qualified lead volume low for a 22-person specialist.

Industry white paper: A well-researched white paper mailed to 210 surveyed managers — covering total cost per kg, the $0.60 green premium tolerance, emissions savings versus diesel and reliability data from 1,380 kg of Q3 trials — would establish AHY as the credible expert, could be forwarded inside fleet boardrooms, and suits the 68% considering a trial within 24 months. Its weakness is passivity: recipients read when convenient, nothing forces a refuelling demo, and technical readers sceptical of hydrogen may never act on paper alone.

Open-day demonstrations: Hosting fleet managers at the corridor station to watch trucks fill in 11 minutes, handle the high-pressure coupling, inspect emissions paperwork and meet the certification team converts the exact objection 47% of managers hold — infrastructure doubt — into firsthand proof. Events generate trial sign-ups on the spot and let AHY qualify leads face to face, though they reach fewer managers per pound than print and need careful safety choreography around live dispensers.

Recommendation: AHY should choose open-day demonstrations, supported by a slim white paper as a follow-up leave-behind. No medium closes the infrastructure objection faster than watching a full-power HGV refuel safely in 11 minutes, and survey evidence says 68% of managers would trial if corridor refuelling proves reliable. Social media is rejected as unqualified reach for a technical B2B sale, and the white paper alone is rejected as too passive to unlock the 47% barrier; the open day turns both into action.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotion options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AHY with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AHY with a well-justified recommendation explaining why social media and the white paper are rejected as standalone choices.

questions.question_text: AHY's small engineering team works under laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for AHY of laissez-faire leadership for its hydrogen engineers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives AHY's highly skilled engineers the autonomy to solve novel high-pressure refuelling problems — dispenser fault diagnosis, trailer hose management, electrolysis scheduling — without waiting for instruction from Dr Vasquez. In a first-of-kind energy pilot there is rarely a textbook, so engineers who can act on their own judgement keep the 11-minute refuelling promise to fleet customers and keep the 78,000 units a year flowing.

Point 2: Autonomy raises job satisfaction and retention among scarce green-hydrogen talent, directly easing the skills gap that leaves 16 of 22 staff without safety certification by keeping certified senior engineers engaged as mentors. A flat structure of self-directing engineers also fits a 22-person organisation where bureaucracy would slow trials, encourages experimentation with mobile trailer logistics, and mirrors the founder's own research-led culture from 2021.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AHY's skills gap, flat structure and pilot trials.

questions.question_text: AHY must certify 16 of its 22 staff on high-pressure hydrogen safety. Consider on-the-job safety coaching at the station or off-the-job courses at the energy skills centre. Which should AHY choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job safety coaching: Coaching at the live corridor station teaches exactly the 350-bar dispenser, venting and emergency shutdown routines used on AHY's equipment, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the station staffed while certification is built — critical with zero customer complaints to defend and the mobile refuelling trailer launching. Drawbacks are that coaching quality depends entirely on whoever is already certified, unsafe shortcuts can be normalised, and no portable certificate results, which insurers, the highways authority and fleet procurement teams may demand before contracting trial capacity.

Off-the-job training: The energy skills centre course at $950 per employee gives all 16 staff structured high-pressure hydrogen safety theory and assessed practical work, certifying them collectively for $15,200 — about 2.4% of the $640,000 investment. Removing 16 of 22 staff from duties is a real operational hit, however, and generic centre procedures will not cover AHY's specific dispenser configuration, mobile trailer marshalling or corridor liaison, so consolidation sessions back at the station remain necessary.

Decision: AHY should choose the off-the-job energy skills centre course for all 16 staff, with short on-the-job consolidation drills afterwards. Hydrogen failures are not forgiving, and a recognised certificate is effectively the licence to scale the corridor trials and win the fleet contracts 68% of managers are ready to sign; the $15,200 fee is trivial against that opportunity. Pure on-the-job coaching is rejected because it leaves AHY uncertified, uninsurable and uncontracted precisely when chain-of-responsibility questions are under scrutiny.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to AHY.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of AHY.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of AHY with a well-justified decision covering cost, safety, compliance and certification.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how AHY's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $176,000 ÷ ($9.50 − $6.30) = $176,000 ÷ $3.20 = 55,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 55,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.50 − $6.30 = $3.20. Answer: contribution per unit is $3.20.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways AHY's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. AHY's managers can compare the 55,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 78,000 units to confirm the corridor station is profitable, with a margin of safety of 23,000 units, informing whether the mobile trailer can operate independently of station volumes.
2. Contribution per unit of only $3.20 warns managers that small cost or price changes dominate profit — for example a $0.30 rise in electrolysis electricity repriced into $6.30 cuts contribution to $2.90 — so they must hedge power contracts or pass costs to fleet contracts.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $176,000 and contribution per unit helps managers model pilot pricing for the 210 surveyed managers, testing whether guaranteeing the $0.60 green premium still covers trials before the second dispenser opens.
4. Managers can use average total cost of $8.56 ($176,000 ÷ 78,000 + $6.30) to benchmark hydrogen delivered cost against diesel after the 8.2% carbon levy, sharpen the corridor pricing story, and set productivity targets of roughly 3,545 units per employee against AHY's 22-person team.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 55,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $3.20 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 23,000 units vs 78,000-unit output; sensitivity modelling of the thin $3.20 contribution against electricity inflation; trial and green-premium pricing strategy for HGV fleet contracts; and average total cost benchmarking at $8.56 against diesel after the carbon levy.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AHY's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has AHY's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue = $1,500,000 and gross profit = $525,000 against cost of sales of $975,000; 2025 revenue = $1,900,000 and gross profit = $760,000 against cost of sales of $1,140,000. 2024 operating profit = $150,000 against $1,500,000 of revenue (10.0%); 2025 operating profit = $266,000 against $1,900,000 of revenue (14.0%). 2024 capital employed = $1,250,000, 2025 = $1,520,000; interest payable rose from $40,000 to $52,000. 2024 figure: $150,000 ÷ $1,250,000 = 12.0% on capital employed; 2025 figure: $266,000 ÷ $1,520,000 = 17.5%.

Evaluation: AHY's profitability has strengthened. Margins widened because revenue grew $400,000 while cost of sales grew only $165,000, showing the station is winning repeat HGV fleet business at sustainable pricing rather than buying volume with discounts. Operating profit rose by $116,000, comfortably outpacing the $12,000 rise in interest payable even after the base rate move. However, capital employed grew 21.6% from $1,250,000 to $1,520,000 — the second dispenser and mobile trailer must now deliver volume, and the 13.7% rise in electrolysis electricity threatens the margin if not hedged. Zero-complaint service quality also depends on curing the certification skills gap before trials convert to long-term contracts.

Conclusion: AHY's financial performance has improved. Gross profit margin rose from 35.0% to 40.0%, the operating profit margin rose from 10.0% to 14.0%, and ROCE rose from 12.0% to 17.5%. The trend supports the $640,000 expansion, but sustaining it requires controlling electricity costs, completing staff certification and converting the 68% trial intent into signed fleet agreements.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether AHY's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for AHY of introducing the second high-pressure dispenser and mobile refuelling trailer on the industrial corridor.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A second dispenser plus mobile trailer removes the single biggest objection holding back hydrogen adoption — 47% of surveyed managers cite lack of refuelling infrastructure — and lets AHY serve the 68% of HGV fleet managers planning trials within 24 months, whether they refuel at the station or need trailer delivery to their depot. It doubles capacity at the corridor, creates a second revenue stream for fleet trials, and positions AHY to lock in green corridor contracts before rival stations emerge.

Disadvantage: The $640,000 investment concentrates AHY's public-company balance sheet into unproven demand, funded partly by a $300,000 bank loan at the new 6.25% base rate. Utilisation could disappoint if the trials slip, leaving fixed costs of $176,000 and the loan repayments uncovered; higher-pressure equipment also raises the stakes of operator error, and with 16 of 22 staff uncertified the mobile trailer cannot operate safely until training completes — a hard dependency the launch timeline must respect.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AHY's research data, costs and certification backlog.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 8.2% carbon levy on diesel, the 13.7% rise in electrolysis electricity costs and the base interest rate rise to 6.25% will affect AHY. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Carbon levy on diesel (8.2%, from January 2027): The levy raises running costs for the conventional diesel HGVs AHY is trying to displace, so every fleet manager maths-checking fuel alternatives sees AHY's green hydrogen become relatively cheaper. It costs AHY nothing directly, strengthens the 68% trial intent recorded in the survey, and could accelerate signed fleet agreements; the risk is that fleets delay buying decisions awaiting subsidy clarity, slowing the very conversion AHY needs.

Electrolysis electricity rise (13.7%): This is a direct cost of making green hydrogen, hitting the $6.30 variable cost that already leaves a thin $3.20 contribution. A 13.7% rise on an electricity component of, say, $3.00 adds about $0.41 per kg, cutting contribution to roughly $2.79; at 78,000 units that is over $32,000 a year of margin pressure unless AHY raises prices, wins the $0.60 green premium, or renegotiates power purchase agreements. It is the largest operational threat to AHY's economics and must be hedged immediately.

Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.25%): Only the $300,000 bank loan is directly affected, adding about $2,250 a year of interest — trivial — and AHY could have financed entirely from the $340,000 share issue instead. Higher rates do make follow-on capital equipment and vehicles more expensive, but the immediate cash impact is the smallest of the three changes.

Conclusion: The 8.2% carbon levy on diesel will have the greatest impact — a positive one. It directly reprices diesel against hydrogen for every HGV operator on the corridor, supercharging the exact conversion wave AHY's trials and second dispenser are built to serve; a 13.7% electricity rise is serious but hedgeable through power contracts. The interest move is negligible at $2,250 a year, and the share issue sidesteps it altogether. AHY should time its launch communications to January 2027, when the levy takes effect and the diesel-to-hydrogen switch becomes urgent for fleet managers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to AHY.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AHY's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AHY with a well-justified judgement that the carbon levy has the greatest (positive) impact and why the other two are smaller or hedgeable.
